To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

feeding dairy cattle a high MS diet, compared with high grass silage, increased milk production and reduced methane emission, and that added NDF increased (and tended to increase) emission from cows fed a high MS diet.
high MS diets increased milk production, but decreased methane emission, whereas added NDF tended to increase methane emission.
cows fed high MS diets had lower methane yield than cows fed high GS diets, and that added NDF increased methane emission and yield of cows fed high MS, but did not affect cows fed high GS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
strategies to increase the efficiency of dairy production systems by increasing milk production per unit of feed consumed and decreasing methane emission from enteric fermentation.
strategies to reduce methane emissions without reducing milk production or profitability of dairy farming, which is an important consideration for adoption of mitigation strategies.
the effect of diet forage sources and neutral detergent fiber on milk production and greenhouse gas emissions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
feeding a high MS versus high GS diet reduced methane emission and yield in dairy cows, and that this effect was not affected by added NDF.

the GF and RC techniques are suitable for measuring methane emission of dairy cows fed different diets and that the GF technique is suitable to measure methane emission in a continuous design, whereas the RC technique requires more time and is more labor intensive, but is more accurate.
high MS diets, without or without added NDF, increased milk production and decreased methane emission compared with high GS diets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the GF and RC techniques for methane emission measurement were comparable in detecting dietary effects on methane emission, and the RC technique was more accurate in measuring individual animal methane emission.
high MS diets increased milk production, whereas GS diets reduced methane emission and methane yield.
high MS diets increased DMI and milk yield, but decreased methane emission compared with high GS diets, and that added NDF to MS diets increased methane emission.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of high MS diets can increase milk production and reduce methane emissions from dairy cattle.
the GF and RC systems can be used interchangeably for measuring methane emissions of dairy cattle fed high forage diets.
high MS diets are associated with greater milk production and lower methane yield than high GS diets.
